answerKey.primaryProblem: Excessive sodium intake and inconsistent carbohydrate intake related to limited food/nutrition-related knowledge, financial constraints, and cultural food patterns, as evidenced by uncontrolled HbA1c (8.5%), Stage II hypertension (155/110), BMI 34, and reported reliance on processed/cured/canned foods.
differential: Excessive sodium intake (NI-5.10.2) related to food/nutrition-related knowledge deficit and cultural food preferences
Inconsistent carbohydrate intake (NI-5.8.4) related to irregular meal pattern (skipped breakfast, convenience lunch) and limited diabetes self-management knowledge
Overweight/obesity (NC-3.3) related to excessive energy intake relative to needs and sedentary lifestyle
Self-monitoring deficit / medication-food interaction knowledge deficit related to self-adjustment of metformin dosing without provider input
keyFindings: HbA1c 8.5% and fasting glucose 145 mg/dL indicate poorly controlled T2DM
BP 155/110 mmHg confirms Stage II hypertension, uncontrolled
BMI 34.0 kg/m2 with 8 lb weight gain over 6 months
Lipid panel shows elevated total cholesterol, LDL, and triglycerides consistent with metabolic syndrome picture
Patient cannot distinguish sodium from salt and does not read nutrition labels
Diet pattern: skipped breakfast, convenience lunch, large sodium-dense family dinner, frequent salty snacking
Self-reported medication non-adherence: skips amlodipine due to leg swelling fear, self-reduced metformin dose due to GI upset without consulting provider
Fluid restriction behavior at work due to urinary frequency, risking dehydration
Financial and time barriers limit access to fresh/lower-sodium foods
Strong cultural attachment to traditional Eastern European foods high in sodium/processed meats/cheese
Bilateral pitting edema and venous distension noted - possible amlodipine side effect vs. fluid status, warrants medical follow-up communication
plan: Educate on sodium vs. salt in simple, concrete terms (e.g., label reading demonstration, teaspoon-to-mg conversion)
Collaboratively identify 1-2 small, sustainable swaps in traditional recipes (e.g., reduce added salt in brining, rinse canned/pickled items, use herbs/spices) rather than eliminating cultural foods
Introduce consistent carbohydrate intake pattern across 3 meals + snacks to support glucose stability; address skipped breakfast
Discuss affordable lower-sodium options (frozen vegetables, no-salt-added canned goods, bulk cooking/batch freezing to address time barrier)
Communicate medication adherence concerns and self-adjusted metformin dose to prescribing provider/PCP for follow-up; do not independently change medication
Provide simple hydration guidance addressing her fear of urinary frequency vs. need for adequate fluid intake
Use motivational interviewing: explore personal motivation (grandchild, energy, avoiding complications), set one SMART small-step goal before next visit
Refer to community resources: Medicaid-covered RD follow-up, local food assistance/SNAP education, diabetes self-management education program, possible social work/financial counseling referral
Schedule follow-up visit to reassess diet log, label-reading skill, and weight/BP trend
Encourage communication with PCP regarding edema and leg swelling possibly related to amlodipine
redFlags: BP 155/110 mmHg meets criteria for Stage II/urgent-range hypertension - needs prompt medical follow-up, not solely nutrition management
HbA1c 8.5% indicates significant hyperglycemia with risk for microvascular complications
Self-adjustment of metformin dose without medical guidance
Medication non-adherence (skipping amlodipine) due to side effect fear
Bilateral pitting edema and venous distension - possible amlodipine-related edema vs. cardiovascular/renal concern requiring medical evaluation
Fluid restriction behavior at work could worsen dehydration and urinary concentration
Visual disturbance (occasional blurred vision) reported - should be flagged to PCP for diabetic eye screening
educationPoints: Clarify that 'sodium' is the specific nutrient on labels; 'salt' (sodium chloride) is the table seasoning - both contribute, but sodium content on nutrition facts panel is the number to track (goal typically <2300 mg/day, ideally closer to 1500 mg for her BP level)
Reducing sodium does not mean giving up traditional foods entirely - portion, frequency, and preparation modifications can preserve cultural connection
Consistent, moderate carbohydrate intake at regular meal times helps stabilize blood glucose better than skipping meals and overeating later
Hydration is important for kidney and blood sugar management; avoiding water due to bathroom concerns can worsen dehydration and urine concentration
Medication side effects should be reported to the prescriber rather than self-adjusting dose, since this can affect both safety and effectiveness
Small, gradual changes (one swap at a time) are more sustainable than an all-or-nothing approach to weight loss

artifacts.title: Endocrinology/PCP Referral Note - New Diagnosis Summary
artifacts.author: Dr. R. Castellano, MD (Primary Care)
artifacts.body: 64 y/o F presents with new diagnosis of Stage II hypertension (BP 155/110 on two separate readings) and poorly controlled Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus (diagnosed 2 years ago, HbA1c 8.5%). Patient reports fatigue, polyuria, polydipsia, intermittent blurred vision, and bilateral ankle swelling. Exam notable for BMI 34, bilateral pitting edema 1+ at ankles, mild venous distension, skin tags at neck/elbow consistent with insulin resistance. Started amlodipine 5mg daily; continuing metformin 500mg BID. Referred to registered dietitian for medical nutrition therapy given new diagnoses and health literacy concerns. Recommend diabetes self-management education referral. Follow-up in 4 weeks to reassess BP and glucose control; will reassess need for additional antihypertensive or antidiabetic agents based on response to lifestyle intervention.

objectives.text: Gather a complete nutrition-focused health history, including assessment of the patient's health literacy and understanding of sodium vs. salt and her chronic conditions.
Perform anthropometric, vital sign, and laboratory assessment and correctly interpret findings in the context of nutrition diagnosis.
Formulate an accurate PES (Problem, Etiology, Signs/Symptoms) statement reflecting excessive sodium intake and inconsistent carbohydrate intake linked to knowledge, cultural, and financial barriers.
Explore medication adherence and self-adjustment behaviors and integrate medication-nutrition interactions into the care plan, escalating concerns to the medical team as appropriate.
Apply motivational interviewing techniques to explore the patient's ambivalence, cultural attachment to traditional foods, and intrinsic motivations for change.
Identify and problem-solve psychosocial and systemic barriers (financial, time, cultural, health literacy) and connect the patient with appropriate interprofessional/community resources.

patient.name: Yvette Armstrong
patient.appearance: Seated at her kitchen table on a laptop camera, wearing work-casual clothing with a cardigan; appears mildly tired with slight under-eye circles; has a cup of tea nearby; occasionally glances off-screen when her phone buzzes, mentioning she's expecting a call from her daughter

persona.personality: Curious, earnest, and eager to learn but easily overwhelmed by technical jargon and lengthy explanations. Values honesty and direct communication. Tries hard to comply but becomes frustrated when changes feel too difficult or unsustainable.
persona.communicationStyle: Asks clarifying questions when confused; may hesitate to ask follow-up questions if she feels she's burdening the provider; responds well to patient, respectful, non-judgmental communication; uses lay terms and needs concepts explained simply with concrete examples.
persona.emotionalState: Anxious and somewhat overwhelmed about new diagnoses, but hopeful and motivated when she feels heard rather than lectured
persona.background: Grew up in a tight-knit Eastern European American family where food was the centerpiece of every gathering - holidays meant pierogis, kielbasa, cabbage rolls, pickled everything. Earned an associate's degree in political science and has worked for the state government for over 20 years in an administrative role. Married with a supportive husband; two adult children live locally and she recently became a grandmother, which she describes as the best thing that's happened to her in years. Involved in local community/political groups in her younger years. Enjoys a small backyard garden and has a dog named Max.
speechExamples: Wait, so sodium and salt aren't the same thing? Nobody ever told me that.
I just don't have an hour to cook every night, you know?
My family's going to think I've gone crazy if I show up to dinner without the kielbasa.
I'm not trying to be difficult, I just don't know where to even start.
Is losing weight really just about starving myself? Because I don't think I can do that.
concerns: Fear of complications from diabetes and hypertension like stroke or heart attack
Worry about medication side effects, especially leg swelling and stomach upset
Frustration with not understanding the difference between sodium and salt
Concern about the cost of healthy food on a tight budget
Anxiety about disappointing or alienating her family by changing traditional eating habits

scenario.studentBrief: You are a dietetics student conducting an initial telehealth nutrition assessment for Yvette Armstrong, a 64-year-old woman recently diagnosed with Stage II hypertension and poorly controlled Type 2 Diabetes (diagnosed 2 years ago), referred by her PCP for medical nutrition therapy. Review the chart before the call. Conduct a nutrition-focused history and assessment, identify barriers to behavior change, and provide patient-centered counseling using motivational interviewing. Document your encounter in ADIME format.
scenario.chiefComplaint: New diagnosis of Stage II hypertension and uncontrolled Type 2 Diabetes; referred for nutrition counseling
scenario.openingLine: Hi, thanks for seeing me - my doctor said I really need to talk to someone about my eating because of my blood pressure and my sugar being high. Honestly, I'm not even sure where to start.
tasks: Conduct a nutrition-focused history including 24-hour recall/typical day, meal pattern, fluid intake, and physical activity
Assess the patient's health literacy and understanding of her conditions, including her confusion about sodium vs. salt
Review labs, vitals, anthropometrics, and medications relevant to nutrition diagnosis
Identify financial, cultural, time, and emotional barriers to dietary change using open-ended, non-judgmental questioning
Formulate a nutrition diagnosis (PES statement) and deliver culturally sensitive, motivational-interviewing-based counseling with a concrete small-step plan
Document the encounter using the ADIME format

profile.setting: Telehealth video visit; patient at home, seated at her kitchen table
profile.summary: A 64-year-old woman with new Stage II hypertension and poorly controlled Type 2 Diabetes presents for an initial telehealth nutrition assessment. The case teaches history-taking around health literacy gaps (sodium vs. salt confusion), identification of cultural/financial/time barriers to dietary change, recognition of medication non-adherence and self-adjustment, and application of motivational interviewing to build a culturally sensitive, sustainable nutrition care plan documented in ADIME format.
profile.title: Nutrition Assessment and Counseling for New Stage II Hypertension and Uncontrolled Type 2 Diabetes in a Health-Literacy-Limited Patient
